items.name: Aaron Levie
items.text: A decent amount of agent adoption and deployment is bottlenecked by being able to test, tune, and optimize agents on “real” work environments. The files agents need to access, the CRM environments, email, and more. It’s impossible to know how agents are performing if you don’t understand how well they’re executing on your evals and how they’ll perform in the future with a model change or workflow upgrade. Every enterprise has to do this 1 by 1 right now, which is obviously slow and tedious. Every enterprise is going to have someone managing evals, infrastructure for building and running evals and simulated environments, and more. Huge space.

items.name: Ryo Lu
items.text: remembering Steve i grew up with beige boxes. then i moved to Canada and saw the iMac G4. how can computers be so beautiful? i couldn’t afford a Mac, so i made my PC look like one. changed the icons, the fonts, the windows. learned to make those shiny, lickable buttons. that’s how i got into interface design. i saw something i loved and wanted to make things like it. i burned DVDs of Steve’s keynotes and studied them. watched them again and again. there was so much care in the products, and so much joy in showing people what they could do. my first iPod was a black nano. i carried it everywhere. then the iPhone happened and changed the world. it felt like anything was possible. since he died, i’ve felt us getting stuck in a loop. constant refinement. better supply chains. more ways to keep people scrolling. so much talent spent on tiny improvements, so little room for something truly great and heartfelt. the keynotes get more cinematic every year. i still miss the live demos. someone onstage playing with something they helped make. the excitement, the jokes, the things that went wrong. it felt human. it was fun. we made computers faster. phones thinner. added more cameras. made machines smarter than us at more and more things. somehow, we’ve also become more disconnected and lonely. we spend so much energy trying to beat humans. i wish we spent more time learning from people’s lives and making them better. when i work, i still sometimes think: what would Steve do? i’ll never know. i’m sad i never got to work with him. but his work reached a kid with a beige PC and changed the course of his life. i wonder how many others have a story like mine. i’ve kept these words with me: “the people who are crazy enough to think they can change the world, are the ones who do.” there’s still so much worth making. things we can put our hearts into. things that make someone feel what i felt when i first saw that iMac. thank you, Steve. 💛

items.name: Guillermo Rauch
items.text: Introducing gdp-ts: Ghosts of Departed Proofs for TypeScript. gdp-ts is a library, linter and AI skill for safer API design. Under this contract, sensitive functions require 'proofs' that the caller performed an authorization check. The typechecker verifies these proofs at compile time, preventing your team and agents from shipping catastrophic security (and other kinds of) bugs. While these patterns have existed for quite some time, especially in ecosystems like Haskell, ① human code review and ② cognitive and syntactic overhead made these solutions niche. The situation is now inverted. Agents are writing more code than we can review, and they *thrive* in tight loops with hard constraints that would frustrate us. We see this with the rise of Rust, borrow checker, code aesthetics debate and all. The README and examples model a real-world Vercel API product constraint: changing the password on a Project requires a proof of a certain role + a certain entitlement. Thanks to Matt Noonan and Ollie Charles for their research in this space. https://t.co/eRWdiMvQ2V
